claim: The hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) maintains neural stem cells (NSCs) and neurogenesis into adulthood.
source: The hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) is a unique brain region maintaining neural stem cells (NCSs) and neurogenesis into adulthood.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Intermediate progenitors (IPs, Tbr2+) pioneered migrations during DG formation.
source: Intermediate progenitors (IPs, Tbr2+) pioneered migrations, supporting and guiding later emigrating NSCs (Sox9+) through multiple transient zones prior to converging at the nascent outer adult niche in a dynamic settling process, generating all prenatal and postnatal granule neurons in defined spatiotemporal order.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data showing Tbr2+ cells in the DMS before Sox9+ NSCs, and by live-cell imaging data.

claim: IPs support and guide later emigrating NSCs (Sox9+) through multiple transient zones.
source: Intermediate progenitors (IPs, Tbr2+) pioneered migrations, supporting and guiding later emigrating NSCs (Sox9+) through multiple transient zones prior to converging at the nascent outer adult niche in a dynamic settling process, generating all prenatal and postnatal granule neurons in defined spatiotemporal order.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging showing IP-NSC interactions and conditional knockout experiments showing NSC migration defects without IPs.

claim: IPs and NSCs converge at the nascent outer adult niche in a dynamic settling process.
source: Intermediate progenitors (IPs, Tbr2+) pioneered migrations, supporting and guiding later emigrating NSCs (Sox9+) through multiple transient zones prior to converging at the nascent outer adult niche in a dynamic settling process, generating all prenatal and postnatal granule neurons in defined spatiotemporal order.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data showing convergence of IP streams at the SGZ.

claim: IPs generate all prenatal and postnatal granule neurons in defined spatiotemporal order.
source: Intermediate progenitors (IPs, Tbr2+) pioneered migrations, supporting and guiding later emigrating NSCs (Sox9+) through multiple transient zones prior to converging at the nascent outer adult niche in a dynamic settling process, generating all prenatal and postnatal granule neurons in defined spatiotemporal order.
evidence: Supported by genetic lineage tracing experiments showing IP-derived neurons at different developmental stages occupy specific layers of the GCL.

claim: IPs (Dll1+) extensively targeted contacts to mitotic NSCs (Notch active).
source: IPs (Dll1+) extensively targeted contacts to mitotic NSCs (Notch active), revealing a substrate for cell-cell contact support during migrations, a developmental feature maintained in adults.
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling showing Dll1+ IPs and Notch-active NSCs, and by live-cell imaging showing IP processes contacting mitotic NSCs.

claim: IP-NSC contact interactions during migration are a developmental feature maintained in adults.
source: IPs (Dll1+) extensively targeted contacts to mitotic NSCs (Notch active), revealing a substrate for cell-cell contact support during migrations, a developmental feature maintained in adults.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data from both embryonic and adult stages showing similar IP behaviors.

claim: Mouse DG formation shares conserved features of human neocortical expansion.
source: Mouse DG formation shares conserved features of human neocortical expansion.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on similarities in IP-NSC dynamics and Notch signaling between DG and neocortex.

claim: The dentate migratory stream (DMS) forms from the dentate neuroepithelial stem zone (DNe) to the developing DG.
source: However, compared to studies of adult DG neurogenesis, studies of DG development are relatively limited. Nonetheless, progenitor cell migration has been a prominently proposed feature, marked classically by formation of the dentate migratory stream (DMS) from the dentate neuroepithelial stem zone (DNe) to the developing DG (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by classical literature and confirmed by the authors' immunolabeling and imaging data.

claim: Progenitor cells in the DMS are distributed in multiple transient niches before settling in the subgranular zone (SGZ).
source: Progenitor cells in the DMS are furthermore distributed in multiple transient (but distinct) niches, presumably migrating to the nascent DG before finally settling in the subgranular zone (SGZ), an enduring niche that persists to youth or adulthood (Figure 1A; Altman and Bayer, 1990a; Altman and Bayer, 1990b; Hodge et al., 2013; Li et al., 2009; Nicola et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by the authors' data showing progenitors in DMS, FDJ, SPNZ, and Hi.

claim: The SGZ is an enduring niche that persists to youth or adulthood.
source: Progenitor cells in the DMS are furthermore distributed in multiple transient (but distinct) niches, presumably migrating to the nascent DG before finally settling in the subgranular zone (SGZ), an enduring niche that persists to youth or adulthood (Figure 1A; Altman and Bayer, 1990a; Altman and Bayer, 1990b; Hodge et al., 2013; Li et al., 2009; Nicola et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The distinct roles and contributions of IPs and NSCs to DG morphogenesis are unknown.
source: The distinct roles and contributions of IPs and NSCs to DG morphogenesis, and the cellular interactions supporting NSC migration and maintenance in the DMS and other DG niches, are unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The cellular interactions supporting NSC migration and maintenance in the DMS and other DG niches are unknown.
source: The distinct roles and contributions of IPs and NSCs to DG morphogenesis, and the cellular interactions supporting NSC migration and maintenance in the DMS and other DG niches, are unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: How multiple streams of migrating progenitor cells differentiate into granule neurons (GNs) and construct the granule cell layer (GCL) in an 'outside-in' mosaic fashion is not clear.
source: Moreover, exactly how multiple streams of migrating progenitor cells differentiate into granule neurons (GNs) and construct the granule cell layer (GCL) in an 'outside-in' mosaic fashion are not clear (Angevine, 1965; Martin et al., 2002).
evidence: This identifies another knowledge gap, referencing classic birthdating studies.

claim: Substantial Eomes+ IP production marked a discrete DNe ventricular patch at E11.5.
source: Surprisingly, substantial Eomes+ IP production marked a discrete DNe ventricular patch even at early stages (E11.5, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data from the Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Eomes+ IPs had accumulated in an outer DNe region near the pial surface by E11.5, defining the DMS origin.
source: Moreover, Eomes+ IPs had already accumulated in an outer DNe region near the pial surface, defining the DMS origin by E11.5 that was even more apparent by E13.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Initial IP production and accumulation in the DNe were readily distinguished from flanking hippocampal CA field and fimbria/choroid plexus stem zones at E13.5.
source: Importantly, initial IP production and accumulation in the DNe were readily distinguished from flanking hippocampal CA field and fimbria/choroid plexus stem zones at E13.5, the latter of which is marked by Lmx1a+ progenitors that give rise to Trp73+ Reln+ Cajal-Retzius cells (CRs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Anstötz and Maccaferri, 2020; Hodge et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The fimbria/choroid plexus stem zone is marked by Lmx1a+ progenitors that give rise to Trp73+ Reln+ Cajal-Retzius cells.
source: Importantly, initial IP production and accumulation in the DNe were readily distinguished from flanking hippocampal CA field and fimbria/choroid plexus stem zones at E13.5, the latter of which is marked by Lmx1a+ progenitors that give rise to Trp73+ Reln+ Cajal-Retzius cells (CRs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Anstötz and Maccaferri, 2020; Hodge et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations and confirmed by the authors' data.

claim: DNe derived Tbr2+ IPs are distinct from hem/fimbria-derived Cajal-Retzius cells at E14.5.
source: Pax6/Tbr2/Reelin triple immunofluorescence at E14.5 reveals distinct DNe derived Tbr2+ IPs (Pax6+/- and Reelin-) in the DMS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), while transient Tbr2 expression overlap is observed as CRs differentiate (Tbr2+ Reelin+) and emerge from the more medial hem/fimbria (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by triple immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: Dll1 expression was highest in the DNe at early stages.
source: Like Eomes expression, Dll1 expression also was highest in the DNe (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overlapping Notch1 and Notch3 receptors and Hes1, Hes5, and Hey1 effector gene expression occurred in E11.5 DNe.
source: Overlapping Notch1 and Notch3 receptors and Hes1, Hes5, and Hey1 effector gene expression occurred in E11.5 DNe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: High Hes5 expression marked the early DNe, likely due to focally increased Lfng expression.
source: Interestingly, high Hes5 expression also marked the early DNe, likely due to focally increased Lfng expression, a key cofactor necessary for processing mature Notch receptors (Semerci et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating high overall Notch signaling activity in the DNe.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data and citation to Semerci et al., 2017.

claim: High Hes5 and Lfng expression in the early DNe indicates high overall Notch signaling activity.
source: Interestingly, high Hes5 expression also marked the early DNe, likely due to focally increased Lfng expression, a key cofactor necessary for processing mature Notch receptors (Semerci et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating high overall Notch signaling activity in the DNe.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression data and knowledge of Notch signaling.

claim: By E13.5, downregulation of Hey1 and concomitant transient upregulation of Hey2 in the DNe was observed.
source: By E13.5 however, downregulation of Hey1 and concomitant transient upregulation of Hey2 in the DNe was observed, which may be in part due to developmental shifts from Notch3 to Notch2 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting multiple temporal combinatorial levels underlie high Notch signaling in the early DNe.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Developmental shifts from Notch3 to Notch2 expression may contribute to changes in Hey1/Hey2 expression.
source: By E13.5 however, downregulation of Hey1 and concomitant transient upregulation of Hey2 in the DNe was observed, which may be in part due to developmental shifts from Notch3 to Notch2 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting multiple temporal combinatorial levels underlie high Notch signaling in the early DNe.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed expression patterns.

claim: Multiple temporal combinatorial levels underlie high Notch signaling in the early DNe.
source: By E13.5 however, downregulation of Hey1 and concomitant transient upregulation of Hey2 in the DNe was observed, which may be in part due to developmental shifts from Notch3 to Notch2 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting multiple temporal combinatorial levels underlie high Notch signaling in the early DNe.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complex expression patterns observed.

claim: Dll1 immunolabeling revealed intense Dll1 protein expression in the DNe at E12.5.
source: Dll1 immunolabeling revealed intense Dll1 protein expression in the DNe at E12.5, validating high Dll1 transcription levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Increased Dll1+/Tbr2+/Tbr2GFP+ and Dll1+/Dll3+ immunolabeling confirmed early IP production and accumulation in the DNe and overlying SVZ at E12.5.
source: Increased Dll1+/Tbr2+/Tbr2GFP+ and Dll1+/Dll3+ immunolabeling confirmed early IP production and accumulation in the DNe and overlying SVZ compared to hem and hippocampal CA field stem zones (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dll3 is a Dll1 homolog marking later stage IPs in neocortex that have begun downregulating Dll1 as IPs further differentiate.
source: Dll3 is a Dll1 homolog marking later stage IPs in neocortex that have begun downregulating Dll1 as IPs further differentiate (Ladi et al., 2005; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Sox9 showed NSCs in the DNe but not the DMS at E12.5, confirming that IPs and not NSCs initially accumulated in the E12.5 SVZ.
source: Sox9 showed NSCs in the DNe but not the DMS, confirming that IPs and not NSCs initially accumulated in the E12.5 SVZ (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hes1 protein levels were relatively high in DNe NSCs at E12.5.
source: Hes1 protein levels were relatively high in DNe NSCs, and were higher in non-mitotic NSCs compared to mitotic NSCs andTbr2GFP+ IPs (Figure 1B, B1), similar to the neocortex (Mizutani et al., 2007; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1B, B1 and citations to previous work.

claim: Hes1 levels were higher in non-mitotic NSCs compared to mitotic NSCs and Tbr2GFP+ IPs.
source: Hes1 protein levels were relatively high in DNe NSCs, and were higher in non-mitotic NSCs compared to mitotic NSCs andTbr2GFP+ IPs (Figure 1B, B1), similar to the neocortex (Mizutani et al., 2007; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1B, B1.

claim: Punctate Dll1 was expressed in Tbr2GFP+ IPs and was notably enriched in their VZ processes, particularly near the ventricular surface.
source: Punctate Dll1 was expressed in Tbr2GFP+ IPs and was notably enriched in their VZ processes, particularly near the ventricular surface (Figure 1B1).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1B1.

claim: NSCs (Tbr2GFP-) exhibited various Hes1+ levels, consistent with heterogeneous, reiterative, and oscillatory signaling.
source: NSCs (Tbr2GFP-) exhibited various Hes1+ levels (Figure 1B1), consistent with heterogeneous, reiterative, and oscillatory signaling (Imayoshi et al., 2013; Nelson et al., 2013; Shimojo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data and citations to previous work on oscillatory Notch signaling.

claim: Hes1-/Dll1+/Tbr2GFP+ IP mitoses were observed in outer VZ/SVZ regions within the intensely Dll1-labeled DNe at E12.5.
source: Interestingly, within the intensely Dll1-labeled DNe, Hes1-/Dll1+/Tbr2GFP+ IP mitoses were observed in outer VZ/SVZ regions, and further distinguishing the DNe from adjacent stem zones at this stage (Figure 1B1).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1B1.

claim: Much Dll1 puncta was present in neighboring Tbr2GFP- progenitors in the DNe, suggesting additional NSC heterogeneity and diversification prior to differentiating into the IP fate.
source: While transgenic labeling allowed us to determine that IPs and their GFP+ processes are a main source of Dll1, much Dll1 puncta was present in neighboring Tbr2GFP- progenitors in the DNe, consistent with its oscillatory regulation and suggesting additional NSC heterogeneity and diversification prior to differentiating into the IP fate (Kawaguchi et al., 2008; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunolabeling data and knowledge of oscillatory Dll1 expression.

claim: By E14.5, the DMS became distinct as a radial extension of the SVZ to the subpial zone.
source: We used more specific molecular markers to identify and locate IPs and NSCs, and by E14.5, the DMS became distinct as a radial extension of the SVZ to the subpial zone (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At E14.5, the DMS contained abundant Tbr2+ IPs, but very few Sox9+ NSCs.
source: At this early stage, the DMS contained abundant Tbr2+ IPs, but very few Sox9+ NSCs (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: Most DMS cells at E14.5 were IPs that co-expressed Tbr2 and Pax6.
source: Most DMS cells were IPs that co-expressed Tbr2 and Pax6 (the latter indicating early-stage IP identity), although a few NSCs (Tbr2-/Pax6+) were seen in the proximal DMS (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A few NSCs (Tbr2-/Pax6+) were seen in the proximal DMS at E14.5.
source: Most DMS cells were IPs that co-expressed Tbr2 and Pax6 (the latter indicating early-stage IP identity), although a few NSCs (Tbr2-/Pax6+) were seen in the proximal DMS (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Early DG IPs transiently express Pax6, similar to neocortical IPs.
source: Hence, early DG IPs transiently express Pax6, similar to neocortical IPs (Englund et al., 2005; Nelson et al., 2013), and likely retain GFP expression from transgenically labeled NesGFP+ NSCs, obfuscating clear IP versus NSC identification.
evidence: Supported by the authors' data and citations to previous work on neocortical IPs.

claim: Early DG IPs likely retain GFP expression from transgenically labeled NesGFP+ NSCs.
source: Hence, early DG IPs transiently express Pax6, similar to neocortical IPs (Englund et al., 2005; Nelson et al., 2013), and likely retain GFP expression from transgenically labeled NesGFP+ NSCs, obfuscating clear IP versus NSC identification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of the NesGFP transgene and IP differentiation.

claim: In the subpial zone at E14.5, the early DMS ran parallel to, but just beneath the marginal zone, where Cajal-Retzius neurons (CRs, Trp73+) migrated from their source in the fimbria towards the hippocampal fissure.
source: In the subpial zone, the early DMS ran parallel to, but just beneath the marginal zone, where Cajal-Retzius neurons (CRs, Trp73+) migrated from their source in the fimbria towards the hippocampal fissure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 2; Hodge et al., 2013; Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by the authors' data and citations to previous work.

claim: By E15.5, Eomes+ IPs accumulated distally to form the DG, just proximal to the hippocampal fissure.
source: By E15.5, Eomes+ IPs accumulated distally to form the DG, just proximal to the hippocampal fissure, by contrast to the DG anlage, which contained very few NSCs (Sox2+) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The DG anlage at E15.5 contained very few NSCs (Sox2+).
source: By E15.5, Eomes+ IPs accumulated distally to form the DG, just proximal to the hippocampal fissure, by contrast to the DG anlage, which contained very few NSCs (Sox2+) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: By E16.5, Sox9+ NSCs were distributed throughout the DMS and some reached the DG anlage.
source: However, by E16.5, Sox9+ NSCs were distributed throughout the DMS and some reached the DG anlage (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The DMS is pioneered by an early cohort of IPs, which 'pave the way' for subsequent NSC migration.
source: Together, these data suggested that the DMS is pioneered by an early cohort of IPs, which seemed to 'pave the way' for subsequent NSC migration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of IP and NSC appearance in the DMS.

claim: From E16.5 to postnatal day 10 (P10), progenitors continuously migrated, occupied, and divided in multiple outer niches including the DMS, FDJ, SPNZ, Hi, and SGZ.
source: From E16.5 to postnatal day 10 (P10), progenitors continuously, migrated, occupied, and divided in multiple outer niches including the DMS, the fimbriodentate junction (FDJ), the subpial neurogenic zone (SPNZ), the hilus (Hi), and the subgranular zone (SGZ) (Figure 1A; Altman and Bayer, 1990a; Angevine, 1965; Hodge et al., 2013; Li et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by the authors' data across multiple time points and citations to previous work.

claim: By E16.5, multiple outer niches (DMS/FDJ/SPNZ/SGZ) were distinguished by IP GFP reporter mice.
source: By E16.5, multiple outer niches (DMS/FDJ/SPNZ/SGZ) were distinguished by IP GFP reporter mice, in this case the knockin EomesGFP/+ line (Arnold et al., 2009), simplified to Tbr2GFP (KI) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B), including abundant mitotic Tbr2+ IPs and Sox9+ NSCs (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data from Tbr2GFP reporter mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B and Figure 1E.

claim: The nascent SGZ at E16.5 was marked by horizontally aligned Tbr2+/Tbr2GFP+ IPs, located just beneath the row of Prox1+ GNs in the newly forming suprapyramidal blade (SPB) of the GCL.
source: The nascent SGZ was marked on E16.5 by the presence of horizontally aligned Tbr2+/Tbr2GFP+ IPs, located just beneath the row of Prox1+ GNs in the newly forming suprapyramidal blade (SPB) of the GCL (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: By E18.5, the expanding SPB was surrounded by multiple contiguous outer niches (DMS, FDJ, SPNZ, Hi, SGZ).
source: By E18.5, the expanding SPB was surrounded by multiple contiguous outer niches (DMS, FDJ, SPNZ, Hi, SGZ) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: NSCs and IPs at E18.5 were located in the overlying SPNZ and appeared to migrate through the nascent SPB, with some accumulating in the nascent SGZ.
source: While NSCs and IPs were located in the overlying SPNZ and appeared to migrate through the nascent SPB, some had accumulated in the nascent SGZ (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1F, G.

claim: Many NSCs in the SPNZ and SGZ at E18.5 were Sox9+/PCNA+, while some were Sox9+/PCNA-, indicating a quiescent NSC state.
source: Co-labeling of Sox9+ NSCs with PCNA, a marker of proliferating cells, showed many NSCs in the SPNZ and SGZ were Sox9+/PCNA+, while some were Sox9+/PCNA-, indicating a quiescent NSC state, especially along the SGZ (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Many Nestin- and/or GFAP-labeled glial processes (and some mitotic figures) were aligned along the DMS at E18.5, but radial processes uniformly spanning the SPB were not yet apparent.
source: While many Nestin- and/or GFAP-labeled glial processes (and some mitotic figures) were aligned along the DMS, radial processes uniformly spanning the SPB were not yet apparent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: By postnatal day 2 (P2), at the peak of GN neurogenesis, the infrapyramidal blade (IPB) of the GCL had begun to form adjacent to the FDJ.
source: By postnatal day 2 (P2), at the peak of GN neurogenesis, the infrapyramidal blade (IPB) of the GCL had begun to form adjacent to the FDJ, and all outer niches contained abundant IPs and NSCs (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: All outer niches at P2 contained abundant IPs and NSCs.
source: By postnatal day 2 (P2), at the peak of GN neurogenesis, the infrapyramidal blade (IPB) of the GCL had begun to form adjacent to the FDJ, and all outer niches contained abundant IPs and NSCs (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Many mitotic figures were seen at P2, including Tbr2+ IPs dividing in the nascent SGZ and Tbr2+/Sox+/Pax6+ mitotic figures (transition from NSC to IP) in the FDJ.
source: Many mitotic figures were seen, for example, Tbr2+ IPs dividing in the nascent SGZ (Figure 1H) and Tbr2+/Sox+/Pax6+ mitotic figures (transition from NSC to IP) in the FDJ (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1H, I.

claim: By P10, the GCL displayed adult-like morphology, and the SGZ was distinct with abundant Sox9+ NSCs and Tbr2+ IPs.
source: By P10, the GCL displayed adult-like morphology, and the SGZ was distinct with abundant Sox9+ NSCs and Tbr2+ IPs (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Many Sox9+ NSCs in the SGZ at P10 exhibited a prominent single GFAP+ radial process that branched in the GCL, like 'type I' NSCs in adult hippocampus.
source: Many Sox9+ NSCs in the SGZ exhibited a prominent single GFAP+ radial process that branched in the GCL (Figure 1K) like 'type I' NSCs in adult hippocampus (Nicola et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1K and citation to Nicola et al., 2015.

claim: Conventional astrocyte (multipolar) proliferation was active around P10.
source: Conventional astrocyte (multipolar) proliferation was also active around P10 (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: From P10 on, IP and NSC proliferation gradually decreased in outer transient niches until P21-P28, when the SGZ became the only remaining outer niche.
source: From P10 on, IP and NSC proliferation gradually decreased in outer transient niches until P21-P28, when the SGZ became the only remaining outer niche (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, though data are not shown.

claim: Outer neurogenic niches in the developing DG are highly dynamic and progress by migration of IPs followed by NSCs.
source: These data suggest that outer neurogenic niches in the developing DG are highly dynamic, and essentially progress by migration of IPs followed by NSCs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the temporal and spatial data presented.

claim: The SGZ arises as part of the process of IP and NSC migration and contains not only IPs but also NSCs (both proliferative and quiescent) at mid-to-late embryonic periods in mice.
source: The SGZ arises as part of this process, and contains not only IPs but also NSCs (both proliferative and quiescent) at mid-to-late embryonic periods in mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the immunolabeling data showing different progenitor types in the SGZ.

claim: The primary role of IPs in formation of the DMS and other outer niches suggests that IPs are required to create a suitable niche for NSC maintenance and proliferation.
source: The primary role of IPs in formation of the DMS and other outer niches further suggested that IPs are required to create a suitable niche for NSC maintenance and proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference that leads to the hypothesis tested with conditional knockout experiments.

claim: High Hes5GFP reporting was found in the fimbria at E14.5.
source: We examined transgenic Hes5GFP reporter mice at E14.5 to visualize NSCs and Notch signaling, and found high reporting in the fimbria and mosaic Hes5GFP labeling in the DNe (Figure 2B; Basak and Taylor, 2007; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by imaging data from Hes5GFP reporter mice shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mosaic Hes5GFP labeling was found in the DNe at E14.5.
source: We examined transgenic Hes5GFP reporter mice at E14.5 to visualize NSCs and Notch signaling, and found high reporting in the fimbria and mosaic Hes5GFP labeling in the DNe (Figure 2B; Basak and Taylor, 2007; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by imaging data from Hes5GFP reporter mice shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Dll1 immunolabeling of Hes5GFP+ sections at E14.5 revealed punctate Dll1 protein in the DNe VZ and SVZ.
source: Dll1 immunolabeling of Hes5GFP+ sections revealed punctate Dll1 protein in the DNe VZ and SVZ (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Within the DNe at E14.5, mosaic Hes5GFP marked subsets of mitotic Pax6high+ NSCs surrounded by punctate Dll1, and asymmetric divisions were apparent.
source: Within the DNe, mosaic Hes5GFP marked subsets of mitotic Pax6high+ NSCs surrounded by punctate Dll1, and asymmetric divisions were apparent (Figure 2B1).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2B1.

claim: NSCs (Hes5GFP+/Pax6+/Dll-) in the outer VZ/SVZ at E14.5 contacted Dll1+ early IPs (Hes5GFP-/Pax6+).
source: NSCs (Hes5GFP+/Pax6+/Dll-) in the outer VZ/SVZ contacted Dll1+ early IPs (Hes5GFP-/Pax6+) (Figure 2B2).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2B2.

claim: Some Hes5GFP+ NSCs were present in the proximal DMS at E14.5, trailing the pioneer Tbr2+ Dll1+ IPs.
source: Some Hes5GFP+ NSCs were present in the proximal DMS (Figure 2B2), trailing the pioneer Tbr2+ Dll1+ IPs, and distinct from Tbr2+/Tbr1+ CRs generated in the fimbria and overlying migration routes (Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2B2, 2C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some Tbr2+ Dll1+ Hes5GFP+ pioneering IPs were observed in the proximal DMS at E14.5.
source: Some Tbr2+ Dll1+ Hes5GFP+ pioneering IPs were also observed in the proximal DMS (Figure 2C), consistent with previous observations in the neocortex, likely due to rapid cell fate changes and GFP stability (Basak and Taylor, 2007; Nelson et al., 2013), although IPs due retain proliferative potential that could be further modulated.
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2C and citations to previous work.

claim: By E15.5, Hes5GFP+ NSCs were more abundant in the DMS, and some exhibited long leading processes.
source: By E15.5, Hes5GFP+ NSCs were more abundant in the DMS, and some exhibited long leading processes (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Hes5GFP+ NSC migrations follow Dll1+ IPs.

claim: Notch activation is maintained during NSC migrations to outer regions.
source: These data confirm that Hes5GFP+ NSC migrations follow Dll1+ IPs, and illustrate that Notch activation is maintained during NSC migrations to outer regions, a notion supported by scattered expression of Notch1, Dll1, Hes5, and Hey2 in the E15.5 DMS (Figure 2A–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by expression data and Hes5GFP reporter data.

claim: Many Dll1+ and/or Dll3+ Tbr2GFP+ IPs were present throughout all transient outer migration routes and neurogenic niches including the nascent SGZ at E16.5.

claim: A few Dll1+/NesGFP+ NSCs were observed near the FDJ and SPNZ at E16.5.
