claim: Dll3+/NesGFP+ cells at E16.5 were rare and most likely represent residual GFP protein in IPs.
source: We examined sections from E16.5 NesGFP+ embryos and observed a few Dll1+/NesGFP+ NSCs near the FDJ and SPNZ, while Dll3+/NesGFP+ cells were rare and most likely represent residual GFP protein in IPs (Figures 2F1–4; Hodge et al., 2013; Mignone et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of the NesGFP transgene and IP differentiation.

claim: Many NesGFP+ NSCs with leading processes were aligned horizontally along the SPNZ at E16.5.
source: Many NesGFP+ NSCs with leading processes were aligned horizontally along the SPNZ (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: An array of NSCs located in the nascent E16.5 SGZ had their GFP-filled processes aligned radially through the underlying SPB.
source: Interestingly, we also observed an array of NSCs located in the nascent E16.5 SGZ with their GFP-filled processes aligned radially through the underlying SPB (Figure 2), suggesting some NSCs have already begun transitioning into adult-like morphologies.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some NSCs at E16.5 have already begun transitioning into adult-like morphologies.
source: Interestingly, we also observed an array of NSCs located in the nascent E16.5 SGZ with their GFP-filled processes aligned radially through the underlying SPB (Figure 2), suggesting some NSCs have already begun transitioning into adult-like morphologies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphology of NSCs observed at E16.5.

claim: On P28, expression of Dll1, Lfng, Hes5, Notch1, and Notch2 were all prominently expressed in the SGZ.
source: On P28, expression of Dll1, Lfng, Hes5, Notch1, and Notch2 were all prominently expressed in the SGZ, indicating a high degree of Notch signaling activity (Figure 2A, S1C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Prominent expression of Dll1, Lfng, Hes5, Notch1, and Notch2 in the P28 SGZ indicates a high degree of Notch signaling activity.
source: On P28, expression of Dll1, Lfng, Hes5, Notch1, and Notch2 were all prominently expressed in the SGZ, indicating a high degree of Notch signaling activity (Figure 2A, S1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression data and knowledge of Notch signaling.

claim: On P35, punctate Dll1 immunolabeling was observed on some NesGFP+ cells (NSCs or early IPs).
source: On P35, punctate Dll1 immunolabeling was observed on some NesGFP+ cells (NSCs or early IPs) (Figure 2G), and on many Tbr2GFP+ IPs (some also Dll3+) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: On P35, punctate Dll1 immunolabeling was observed on many Tbr2GFP+ IPs (some also Dll3+).
source: On P35, punctate Dll1 immunolabeling was observed on some NesGFP+ cells (NSCs or early IPs) (Figure 2G), and on many Tbr2GFP+ IPs (some also Dll3+) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: During initial stages of DG development, Notch activity is highest in early DNe compared to other hippocampal and neocortical niches.
source: These data indicate: 1) During initial stages of DG development, Notch activity is highest in early DNe compared to other hippocampal and neocortical niches; 2) DNe NSCs have higher Notch activity compared to IPs; 3) IPs are the primary Dll1 source during migrations through outer niches; and 4) adult IPs express Dll1 and thus maintain Notch signaling potential.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the expression and reporter data.

claim: DNe NSCs have higher Notch activity compared to IPs.
source: These data indicate: 1) During initial stages of DG development, Notch activity is highest in early DNe compared to other hippocampal and neocortical niches; 2) DNe NSCs have higher Notch activity compared to IPs; 3) IPs are the primary Dll1 source during migrations through outer niches; and 4) adult IPs express Dll1 and thus maintain Notch signaling potential.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on Hes1 immunolabeling and Hes5GFP reporter data.

claim: IPs are the primary Dll1 source during migrations through outer niches.
source: These data indicate: 1) During initial stages of DG development, Notch activity is highest in early DNe compared to other hippocampal and neocortical niches; 2) DNe NSCs have higher Notch activity compared to IPs; 3) IPs are the primary Dll1 source during migrations through outer niches; and 4) adult IPs express Dll1 and thus maintain Notch signaling potential.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on Dll1 immunolabeling data.

claim: Adult IPs express Dll1 and thus maintain Notch signaling potential.
source: These data indicate: 1) During initial stages of DG development, Notch activity is highest in early DNe compared to other hippocampal and neocortical niches; 2) DNe NSCs have higher Notch activity compared to IPs; 3) IPs are the primary Dll1 source during migrations through outer niches; and 4) adult IPs express Dll1 and thus maintain Notch signaling potential.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on Dll1 immunolabeling data from P35 mice.

claim: High focal Notch activity and production of basally accumulating IPs occur prior to NSC migration to, and expansion in outer regions that lead to morphological changes in DG, as in neocortical gyrus formation.
source: Altogether, these findings support the idea that high focal Notch activity and production of basally accumulating IPs occur prior to NSC migration to, and expansion in outer regions that lead to morphological changes in DG, as in neocortical gyrus formation (Llinares-Benadero and Borrell, 2019).
evidence: This is a summary inference drawing parallels to neocortical development, supported by citation.

claim: In E16.5 DNe, IPs extended dynamic processes into the VZ, presumably to interact with NSCs (GFP-).
source: In E16.5 DNe, IPs extended dynamic processes into the VZ (Figure 3A, Video 1), presumably to interact with NSCs (GFP-), similar to IP→NSC interactions in the neocortical VZ (Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Video 1.

claim: IPs in the DNe SVZ withdrew VZ-processes, extended a new outwardly directed dynamically branching leading process, and began migrating into the DMS.
source: Next, IPs in the DNe SVZ withdrew VZ-processes, extended a new outwardly directed dynamically branching leading process, and began migrating into the DMS (Figure 3A3, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A3 and Video 1.

claim: IPs exhibited coordinated migrations within the DMS, migrating along the fimbria and extending processes into, but never entering this region.
source: IPs exhibited coordinated migrations within the DMS, migrating along the fimbria and extending processes into, but never entering this region (Figure 3A2, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A2 and Video 1.

claim: IPs migrating in the DMS contacted neighboring mitotic progenitors, including other IPs and NSCs (Tbr2GFP-).
source: IPs migrating in the DMS contacted neighboring mitotic progenitors, including other IPs and NSCs (Tbr2GFP-, visible by negative contrast) (Figure 3A4-6, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A4-6 and Video 1.

claim: Most early IPs at E16.5 accumulated in the FDJ then continued to migrate and proliferate into the SPNZ, although a few IPs turned from the FDJ into the Hi.
source: Distally, most early IPs accumulated in the FDJ then continued to migrate and proliferate into the SPNZ, although a few IPs turned from the FDJ into the Hi (Figure 3A7, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A7 and Video 2.

claim: By E17.5, many IP mitoses were observed in the DMS→FDJ→SPNZ, and in the inner migration route through the Hi, with inner IPs tracking towards outer IPs at the leading edge of the SPB.
source: By E17.5, many IP mitoses were observed in the DMS→FDJ→SPNZ, and in the inner migration route through the Hi, with inner IPs tracking towards outer IPs at the leading edge of the SPB (Figure 3B1, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3B1 and Video 2.

claim: From the SPNZ at E17.5, horizontally migrating IPs turned inward to migrate radially toward the upper layer of the developing SPB, and IP migration trajectories aligned along the inner edge of the SPB upon reaching the nascent SGZ.
source: From the SPNZ, horizontally migrating IPs turned inward to migrate radially toward the upper layer of the developing SPB, and IP migration trajectories aligned along the inner edge of the SPB upon reaching the nascent SGZ (Figure 3B2, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3B2 and Video 2.

claim: Large-scale morphogenic movements were observed in several slice culture imaging sessions resembling 'gyrification in vitro'.
source: Interestingly, we observed large-scale morphogenic movements in several slice culture imaging sessions resembling 'gyrification in vitro' (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Video 2.

claim: By E18.5, IP radial migrations through the SPB, and IP horizontal migrations within the SGZ were even more prominent.
source: By E18.5, IP radial migrations through the SPB, and IP horizontal migrations within the SGZ were even more prominent (Figure 3C1-2, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3C1-2 and Video 3.

claim: Temporally distinct developmentally born IP cohorts migrating in different routes (SPNZ→SGZ and DMS→hilus) converged at the SGZ by E18.5.
source: Moreover, temporally distinct developmentally born IP cohorts migrating in different routes (SPNZ→SGZ and DMS→hilus) converged at the SGZ (Figure 3C3, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3C3 and Video 3.

claim: Live-cell imaging data reveal the cellular basis for coordinated migration from the DNe into the DMS.
source: These data reveal the cellular basis for coordinated migration from the DNe into the DMS, and a novel substrate for cell-cell contact dependent signaling mechanisms between migrating IPs and NSCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging findings.

claim: Live-cell imaging data reveal a novel substrate for cell-cell contact dependent signaling mechanisms between migrating IPs and NSCs.
source: These data reveal the cellular basis for coordinated migration from the DNe into the DMS, and a novel substrate for cell-cell contact dependent signaling mechanisms between migrating IPs and NSCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging findings showing IP-NSC contacts.

claim: 2-color multiphoton live-cell imaging at E17.5 revealed IP (GFP+/RFP+) migrations and IP-IP interactions during mitosis in the DMS→FDJ→SPNZ.
source: Nevertheless, 2-color multiphoton live-cell imaging revealed IP (GFP+/RFP+) migrations and IP-IP interactions during mitosis in the DMS→FDJ→SPNZ (Figure 4A–B, Video 4).
evidence: Supported by 2-color live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4A-B and Video 4.

claim: 2-color imaging revealed IP interactions and migrations near developing vasculature.
source: Moreover, new views of IP interactions and migrations were seen near developing vasculature (Figure 4D, Video 4), revealing similar interactions as in developing neocortex (Stubbs et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by 2-color live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4D and Video 4.

claim: Multiple live NSC mitoses (GFP-/RFP+) were observed in the FDJ, SPNZ and the nascent SGZ at E17.5, with all receiving extensive IP contacts during mitosis.
source: Multiple live NSC mitoses (GFP-/RFP+) were observed in the FDJ, SPNZ and the nascent SGZ (Figure 4A) with all receiving extensive IP contacts during mitosis (Figure 4C, Video 4).
evidence: Supported by 2-color live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4A, 4C and Video 4.

claim: Many NSCs and IPs had accumulated in the nascent SGZ at E17.5.
source: Orthogonal views revealed many NSCs and IPs had accumulated in the nascent SGZ (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by 2-color live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Computationally rendering two neighboring IP-NSC pairs in the SGZ showed extensive and prolonged, but likely transient contacts.
source: Computationally rendering two neighboring IP-NSC pairs in the SGZ showed extensive and prolonged, but likely transient contacts (Figure 4E,F, Video 4).
evidence: Supported by 2-color live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4E, F and Video 4.

claim: As one NSC extended a radial process through the overlying GCL, the paired IP elaborated its leading process aligned along the SGZ, prior to migrating after prolonged somal interactions.
source: For example, in one pair (Figure 4,F1), as the NSC extended a radial process through the overlying GCL, the IP elaborated its leading process aligned along the SGZ, prior to migrating after prolonged somal interactions (Video 4).
evidence: Supported by 2-color live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4F1 and Video 4.

claim: A non-migrating multipolar IP with extensive long-range processes interacted with multiple niche-localized cells, as well as directly with a neighboring mitotic NSC.
source: In the other pair (Figure 4,F2), a non-migrating multipolar IP with extensive long-range processes interacted with multiple niche-localized cells, as well as directly with a neighboring mitotic NSC (Video 4).
evidence: Supported by 2-color live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4F2 and Video 4.

claim: NSCs were observed migrating horizontally in the DMS.
source: We also observed NSCs migrating horizontally in the DMS (Figure 4G, Video 4), and surprisingly, additional NSCs with leading processes aligned and migrating in a coordinated fashion along the Z-Y axis, in a posterior-to-anterior direction in orthogonal views of coronal slices (Figure 4H–I, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by 2-color live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4G and Video 4.

claim: Additional NSCs with leading processes aligned and migrated in a coordinated fashion along the Z-Y axis, in a posterior-to-anterior direction in orthogonal views of coronal slices.
source: We also observed NSCs migrating horizontally in the DMS (Figure 4G, Video 4), and surprisingly, additional NSCs with leading processes aligned and migrating in a coordinated fashion along the Z-Y axis, in a posterior-to-anterior direction in orthogonal views of coronal slices (Figure 4H–I, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by 2-color live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4H-I and Video 5.

claim: En face multiphoton live-cell imaging revealed laterally (horizontal) directed IP and NSC migrations through the FDJ→SPNZ route.
source: This type of imaging revealed laterally (horizontal) directed IP and NSC migrations through the FDJ→SPNZ route as described, including many migrations near overlying vasculature (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by en face live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Video 5.

claim: En face imaging revealed a sub-population of progenitors aligned longitudinally and migrating near the DMS→FDJ region, confirming postero-anterior migration trajectories from coronal slice imaging.
source: En face imaging also revealed a sub-population of progenitors aligned longitudinally and migrating near the DMS→FDJ region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 5), confirming postero-anterior migration trajectories from coronal slice imaging (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: Supported by en face live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Video 5.

claim: 2-color multiphoton live-cell imaging data reveal IPs directly interact with NSCs during migrations through transient outer neurogenic niches to establish the nascent SGZ.
source: These 2-color multiphoton live-cell imaging data reveal IPs directly interact with NSCs during migrations through transient outer neurogenic niches to establish the nascent SGZ, and provide evidence for possible additional pathways of NSC and IP migration during DG formation (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of the 2-color live-cell imaging findings.

claim: 2-color imaging provides evidence for possible additional pathways of NSC and IP migration during DG formation.
source: These 2-color multiphoton live-cell imaging data reveal IPs directly interact with NSCs during migrations through transient outer neurogenic niches to establish the nascent SGZ, and provide evidence for possible additional pathways of NSC and IP migration during DG formation (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the observation of longitudinal migrations.

claim: By P3, most IPs migrated directly towards the SGZ through the internal DMS→FDJ→Hi route.
source: By P3, most IPs migrated directly towards the SGZ through the internal DMS→FDJ→Hi route, although proliferative IPs remained in the SPNZ and continued their migrations horizontally around the SPB - IBP and through the GCL to the SGZ (Figure 5A, Video 6).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5A and Video 6.

claim: Proliferative IPs remained in the SPNZ at P3 and continued their migrations horizontally around the SPB-IPB and through the GCL to the SGZ.
source: By P3, most IPs migrated directly towards the SGZ through the internal DMS→FDJ→Hi route, although proliferative IPs remained in the SPNZ and continued their migrations horizontally around the SPB - IBP and through the GCL to the SGZ (Figure 5A, Video 6).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5A and Video 6.

claim: IP mitoses were more apparent in the Hi-SGZ region at P3, and IPs migrated laterally within the SGZ and vertically into the GCL or Hi.
source: IP mitoses were more apparent in the Hi-SGZ region, and IPs migrated laterally within the SGZ and vertically into the GCL or Hi (Figure 5A, Video 6).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5A and Video 6.

claim: Converging IP cohorts migrated through outer niches to continually settle the SGZ.
source: Thus, converging IP cohorts migrated through outer niches, to continually settle the SGZ.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the live-cell imaging data.

claim: IP migration speeds were comparable across different groups at P3, but IPs in the DMS migrated farther in a directionally coordinated fashion during the imaging duration.
source: Quantification of different IP groups indicated while IP migration speeds were comparable, IPs in the DMS migrated farther in a directionally coordinated fashion during the imaging duration (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: IPs in all groups (and ages) exhibited similar 'stop and go' migrations, probing with leading processes while paused, followed by rapid re-engagement of migration machinery.
source: Interestingly, IPs in all groups (and ages) exhibited similar 'stop and go' migrations, exemplified by individual IP DMS cell tracks (Figure 5B), probing with leading processes while paused, followed by rapid re-engagement of migration machinery.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data and quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: En face multiphoton live-cell imaging at P4-5 confirmed a longitudinal orientation shift in IP migrations in the postnatal DMS.
source: Also, en face multiphoton live-cell imaging at P4-5 confirmed a longitudinal orientation shift in IP migrations in the postnatal DMS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by en face live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Video 5.

claim: By P12 and P22, IP migrations and mitoses are confined to the SGZ.
source: In late postnatal DG (P7-P22), IP proliferation and migrations remained evident (Video 7), but were increasingly restricted to the SGZ from P12 to P22 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5C and Video 7.

claim: Quantification of all live IP mitoses indicated peak proliferation occurred during late embryonic to early postnatal period.
source: Quantification of all live IP mitoses indicated peak proliferation occurred during late embryonic to early postnatal period (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the more mature P14-P22 DG, IPs continued to migrate within the SGZ, and extensive transient IP long-range dynamic interactions remained.
source: In the more mature P14-P22 DG, IPs also continued to migrate within the SGZ, and extensive transient IP long-range dynamic interactions remained the rule (Figure 5E1-4, Video 7).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5E1-4 and Video 7.

claim: IP processes extended distances up to 100–150 μm and displayed complex branching morphologies in the P14-P22 SGZ.
source: IP processes extended distances up to 100–150 μm and displayed complex branching morphologies, presumably interacting with multiple cell types along the SGZ, including mitotic IPs (Figure 5E1-4, Video 7).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5E1-4 and Video 7.

claim: IPs in the mature SGZ niche continue migratory and dynamic cell-cell interaction behaviors similar to embryonic IPs.
source: Altogether, our live-slice observations open an unprecedented high-resolution window into the cellular basis for DG morphogenesis, and reveal that IPs in the mature SGZ niche continue migratory and dynamic cell-cell interaction behaviors similar to embryonic IPs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on comparison of live-cell imaging data across developmental stages.

claim: Tbr2 is critical for IP differentiation, function, and survival during DG development and adult neurogenesis.
source: Our previous studies showed that Tbr2 is critical for IP differentiation, function, and survival during DG development and adult neurogenesis (Hodge et al., 2013; Hodge et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: At E14.5, many pioneering Tbr2+ IPs were present in the DMS and accompanied by rare Sox9+ NSCs in controls.
source: At E14.5, while many pioneering Tbr2+ IPs were present in the DMS and accompanied by rare Sox9+ NSCs in controls, only a few Tbr2+ IPs that escaped conditional deletion were present in the Tbr2 cKO DMS (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data from control and Tbr2 cKO mice shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Only a few Tbr2+ IPs that escaped conditional deletion were present in the Tbr2 cKO DMS at E14.5.
source: At E14.5, while many pioneering Tbr2+ IPs were present in the DMS and accompanied by rare Sox9+ NSCs in controls, only a few Tbr2+ IPs that escaped conditional deletion were present in the Tbr2 cKO DMS (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data from Tbr2 cKO mice shown in Figure 6A.

claim: By E16.5, the distribution of Sox9+ NSCs was significantly perturbed in Tbr2 cKO DMS.
source: By E16.5, the distribution of Sox9+ NSCs was significantly perturbed in Tbr2 cKO DMS. NSCs appeared disorganized in the proximal DMS, and fewer Sox9+ NSCs reached the distal end of the DMS at the hippocampal fissure (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data from Tbr2 cKO mice shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NSCs appeared disorganized in the proximal DMS in Tbr2 cKO at E16.5, and fewer Sox9+ NSCs reached the distal end of the DMS at the hippocampal fissure.
source: By E16.5, the distribution of Sox9+ NSCs was significantly perturbed in Tbr2 cKO DMS. NSCs appeared disorganized in the proximal DMS, and fewer Sox9+ NSCs reached the distal end of the DMS at the hippocampal fissure (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data from Tbr2 cKO mice shown in Figure 6B.

claim: By E18.5, Sox9+ NSCs were abnormally spread across a wide swath of the proximal DMS in Tbr2 cKO mutants, and the distance NSCs migrated from the ventricular surface was markedly reduced compared to controls.
source: By E18.5, Sox9+ NSCs were abnormally spread across a wide swath of the proximal DMS in Tbr2 cKO DMS mutants, and the distance NSCs migrated from the ventricular surface was markedly reduced compared to controls (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling and quantification data from Tbr2 cKO mice shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: By P2, the pioneering IP cohort and trailing wave of NSCs had successfully migrated in controls to build the SPB and initial segment of IPB.
source: By P2, the pioneering IP cohort and trailing wave of NSCs had successfully migrated in controls to build the SPB and initial segment of IPB (NeuroD1+) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data from control mice shown in Figure 6E.

claim: By P2, severe SPB hypoplasia was apparent in Tbr2 cKO mutants, NSCs appeared delayed in transient DG niches, and the IPB was conspicuously lacking.
source: By contrast, severe SPB hypoplasia was apparent in Tbr2 cKO mutants, NSCs appeared delayed in transient DG niches, and the IPB was conspicuously lacking (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data from Tbr2 cKO mice shown in Figure 6E.

claim: NSCs enter the DMS but fail to coordinately migrate to the definitive DG in Tbr2 cKO mutants, and instead accumulate proximally due to lack of migration cues from Tbr2 cKO depleted IPs in the DMS, followed by their subsequent death and pool depletion.
source: These new findings indicate that NSCs enter the DMS but fail to coordinately migrate to the definitive DG, and instead accumulate proximally due to lack of migration cues from Tbr2 cKO depleted IPs in the DMS, followed by their subsequent death and pool depletion (Hodge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Tbr2 cKO phenotype data and citation to previous work.

claim: Lineage tracing of early IPs (E13.5) to P0.5 demonstrated extensive labeling of Prox1+ GNs, specifically in the outer shell of the SPB.
source: Lineage tracing of early IPs (E13.5) to P0.5 demonstrated extensive labeling of Prox1+ GNs, specifically in the outer shell of the SPB (Figure 7A, A3).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 7A, A3.

claim: E13.5 IP-derived RFP+ cells did not express Tbr2 or Sox9 at P0.5, indicating that none remained as IPs or reverted to NSC identity during the E13.5-P0.5 interval.
source: Significantly, E13.5 IP-derived RFP+ cells did not express Tbr2 or Sox9 (Figure 7, A1-2), indicating that none remained as IPs or reverted to NSC identity during the E13.5-P0.5 interval.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 7A1-2.

claim: Lineage tracing of E16.5 IPs to P0.5 labeled Prox1+ GNs mainly in the outer shell of the IPB, and a smaller number of GNs in the SPB.
source: Similarly, lineage tracing of E16.5 IPs to P0.5 labeled Prox1+ GNs mainly in the outer shell of the IPB, and a smaller number of GNs in the SPB (Figure 7B, B1-3).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 7B, B1-3.

claim: Long-term lineage tracing of early IPs (E13.5-P27) confirmed that pioneering IPs produced GNs in the SPB outer shell, with a sparse distribution reflecting postnatal expansion of the GCL.
source: Long-term lineage tracing of early IPs (E13.5-P27) confirmed that pioneering IPs produced GNs in the SPB outer shell, with a sparse distribution reflecting postnatal expansion of the GCL (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Lineage tracing from P3 (the peak of DG neurogenesis) to P48 demonstrated abundant RFP-labeled GNs within the middle layers of SPB and IPB, sometimes seen as pairs.
source: Lineage tracing from P3 (the peak of DG neurogenesis) to P48 demonstrated abundant RFP-labeled GNs within the middle layers of SPB and IPB, sometimes seen as pairs (Figure 7D, D1-2).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 7D, D1-2.

claim: IP lineage tracing in adult mice (P56 to P84) showed labeled GNs in inner layers of the GCL just outside the SGZ, also sometimes visible as pairs.
source: IP lineage tracing in adult mice (P56 to P84) showed labeled GNs in inner layers of the GCL just outside the SGZ, also sometimes visible as pairs (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: No glial cells were labeled by IP lineage tracing at any age.
source: No glial cells were labeled by IP lineage tracing at any age.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the lineage tracing experiments.

claim: DG IPs exclusively generate all prenatal, postnatal, and adult-born GNs in a defined spatial and temporal developmental order.
source: Overall, these experiments show that DG IPs exclusively generate all prenatal, postnatal, and adult-born GNs in a defined spatial and temporal developmental order (Figure 7F), consistent with previous cell-birthdating and chimera studies (Angevine, 1965; Martin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a summary of the lineage tracing data, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DG formation captures many essential and generalizable principles applicable to other migrating progenitor systems in the developing brain, such as neocortical gyrification.
source: Although the DG is a highly specialized part of the hippocampus, its formation captures many essential and generalizable principles applicable to other migrating progenitor systems in the developing brain, such as neocortical gyrification.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Fundamental principles of DG formation include coordinated migration of IPs and NSCs, maintenance of outer NSCs, and de novo tissue assembly in specific regions.
source: These fundamental principles include coordinated migration of IPs and NSCs, maintenance of outer NSCs, and de novo tissue assembly in specific regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings from the study.

claim: IPs interact with mitotic and migrating NSCs throughout all stages of DG development.
source: Our results indicate that IPs interact with mitotic and migrating NSCs throughout all stages of DG development, revealing a new cellular substrate for actively transmitting contact-dependent signals, and show that IPs are required to pioneer the DMS and to support NSCs in outer niches.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging and conditional knockout findings.

claim: IPs are required to pioneer the DMS and to support NSCs in outer niches.
source: Our results indicate that IPs interact with mitotic and migrating NSCs throughout all stages of DG development, revealing a new cellular substrate for actively transmitting contact-dependent signals, and show that IPs are required to pioneer the DMS and to support NSCs in outer niches.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the Tbr2 cKO experiments.

claim: These data support a general role for IPs in continuously maintaining NSC pools, prominently through Delta-Notch signaling.
source: Altogether, these data support a general role for IPs in continuously maintaining NSC pools, prominently through Delta-Notch signaling.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the Dll1 expression and Notch reporter data.

claim: These findings support the emerging notion that coordinated migration of IPs and NSCs away from the ventricular surface, along with evolutionary modifications in Notch signaling and cell-cell contact, have played important evolutionary roles mediating cortical expansion and morphogenesis.
source: These findings support the emerging notion that coordinated migration of IPs and NSCs away from the ventricular surface, along with evolutionary modifications in Notch signaling and cell-cell contact, have played important evolutionary roles mediating cortical expansion and morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement connecting the findings to broader evolutionary concepts.

claim: Increased genesis of Dll1-production was linked to Notch activation in NSCs in the early DNe.
source: Thus, increased genesis of Dll1-production was linked to Notch activation in NSCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-expression of Dll1 and Notch signaling components in the DNe.

claim: Both IP accumulation and Notch signaling are thought to contribute to initial steps in neocortical outward expansion and gyrification.
source: Both IP accumulation and Notch signaling are thought to contribute to initial steps in neocortical outward expansion and gyrification (de Juan Romero et al., 2015), and we found the same in DG, summarized in Figure 8A.
evidence: This draws a parallel to neocortical development, supported by citation.

claim: IPs (especially processes) are the major source of Dll1 in developing neocortex.
source: Likewise, IPs (especially processes) are the major source of Dll1 in developing neocortex (Nelson et al., 2013), a prominent source in the DNe, and the major source during outer DG migrations and formation.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by the authors' data in DG.

claim: High Notch activity in the DNe likely reflects the magnitude of rapid cell-fate decisions and proliferation occurring to support the burst of Dll1+/Tbr2+ IP accumulation in the outer VZ and SVZ.
source: High Notch activity likely reflects the magnitude of rapid cell-fate decisions and proliferation occurring in the DNe to support the burst of Dll1+/Tbr2+ IP accumulation in the outer VZ and SVZ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed high Notch activity and IP accumulation.

claim: Progressive switches in Notch receptor and effector composition were observed by E13.5 (loss of Notch3/Hey1, gain of Notch2/Hey2), indicating additional temporal layers of combinatorial Notch activities might contribute to regional specification and outer NSC migrations.
source: By E13.5, progressive switches in Notch receptor and effector composition were observed (loss of Notch3/Hey1, gain of Notch2/Hey2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) indicating additional temporal layers of combinatorial Notch activities might contribute to regional specification and outer NSC migrations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in Notch component expression.

claim: High combinatorial Notch signaling and increased IP genesis/accumulation in outer VZ regions distinguish the early rodent DNe from other hippocampal germinal zones and may play a role in DNe specification.
source: Hence, high combinatorial Notch signaling and increased IP genesis/accumulation in outer VZ regions distinguish the early rodent DNe from other hippocampal germinal zones and may play a role in DNe specification (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the expression and immunolabeling data.

claim: These results reveal surprising evolutionarily conserved factors and steps marking premigratory zones between DNe formation and neocortical expansion.
source: These results reveal surprising evolutionarily conserved factors and steps marking premigratory zones between DNe formation and neocortical expansion (Llinares-Benadero and Borrell, 2019), suggesting further mechanistic insight into mouse DG development, disease, injury and repair can inform human pediatric brain malformations and treatments.
evidence: This is a summary statement connecting the findings to broader evolutionary and clinical implications.

claim: The SGZ is seeded with embryonic NSCs that persist as a source of postnatal and adult neurogenesis.
source: Together, these findings raise the possibility that the SGZ is seeded with embryonic NSCs that persist as a source of postnatal and adult neurogenesis. This interpretation is also supported by recent data showing that embryonic DNe NSCs are the origin for at least some adult DG NSCs (Berg et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of NSCs in the nascent SGZ and supported by citation to recent work.

claim: The SGZ is formed even earlier than proposed previously.
source: These findings suggest that the SGZ is formed even earlier than proposed previously (Nicola et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of the nascent SGZ at E16.5.

claim: Dynamic cellular processes can serve as substrates for contact-dependent signals, such as integrin and Notch.
source: Dynamic cellular processes can serve as substrates for contact-dependent signals, such as integrin and Notch, and are beginning to be elucidated (Betizeau et al., 2013; Kalebic et al., 2019; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IPs rapidly target dynamic processes (Dll1+) to neighboring mitotic progenitors (NSCs and IPs) during migrations and in the adult niche.
source: Importantly, our new live data directly revealed that IPs rapidly target dynamic processes (Dll1+) to neighboring mitotic progenitors (NSCs and IPs) during migrations and in the adult niche.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging findings.

claim: The interesting switch from Notch1/3 receptors in early DNe NSCs to Notch1/2 receptors in migrating and later mature DG NSCs was analogous to the evolutionarily similar role of Notch in expansion of human outer NSCs in the neocortex.
source: The interesting switch from Notch1/3 receptors in early DNe NSCs to Notch1/2 receptors in migrating and later mature DG NSCs (Figure 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), was analogous to the evolutionarily similar role of Notch in expansion of human outer NSCs in the neocortex (Fiddes et al., 2018; Hansen et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawing parallels to human neocortical development, supported by citations.

claim: Conditional genetic ablation of selected Notch components (Dll1, Notch1, Rbpj, Notch2, Lfng) demonstrates Notch activity is essential for DG development and/or adult neurogenesis.
source: Although conditional genetic ablation of selected Notch components (Dll1, Notch1, Rbpj, Notch2, Lfng) demonstrates Notch activity is essential for DG development and/or adult neurogenesis (Breunig et al., 2007; Imayoshi et al., 2010; Kawaguchi et al., 2013; Semerci et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019), phenotypic differences in knockouts along with our data indicate a more complex combinatorial and temporally regulated Notch activity network underlies this process, and that Dll1+ IPs are especially prominent and well positioned to support the bulk of Notch signaling during outer migration of outer NSCs.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous conditional knockout studies.

claim: Phenotypic differences in Notch component knockouts along with the authors' data indicate a more complex combinatorial and temporally regulated Notch activity network underlies DG development.
source: Although conditional genetic ablation of selected Notch components (Dll1, Notch1, Rbpj, Notch2, Lfng) demonstrates Notch activity is essential for DG development and/or adult neurogenesis (Breunig et al., 2007; Imayoshi et al., 2010; Kawaguchi et al., 2013; Semerci et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019), phenotypic differences in knockouts along with our data indicate a more complex combinatorial and temporally regulated Notch activity network underlies this process, and that Dll1+ IPs are especially prominent and well positioned to support the bulk of Notch signaling during outer migration of outer NSCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' data and comparison to previous knockout studies.

claim: Dll1+ IPs are especially prominent and well positioned to support the bulk of Notch signaling during outer migration of outer NSCs.
source: Although conditional genetic ablation of selected Notch components (Dll1, Notch1, Rbpj, Notch2, Lfng) demonstrates Notch activity is essential for DG development and/or adult neurogenesis (Breunig et al., 2007; Imayoshi et al., 2010; Kawaguchi et al., 2013; Semerci et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019), phenotypic differences in knockouts along with our data indicate a more complex combinatorial and temporally regulated Notch activity network underlies this process, and that Dll1+ IPs are especially prominent and well positioned to support the bulk of Notch signaling during outer migration of outer NSCs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the authors' data.

claim: IPs and their dynamic processes serve as a continuous rich Dll1 source, providing robust cell-contact mediated Notch reactivation signals targeting NSCs, maintaining their higher Notch activity and stemness in outer transient niches during DG development, similar to the neocortex.
source: Altogether, our findings support the hypothesis that IPs and their dynamic processes serve as a continuous rich Dll1 source, providing robust cell-contact mediated Notch reactivation signals targeting NSCs, maintaining their higher Notch activity and stemness in outer transient niches during DG development (Figure 8B), similar to the neocortex (Kawaguchi et al., 2013; Kawaguchi et al., 2008; Mizutani et al., 2007; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings, drawing parallels to neocortex and supported by citations.

claim: Adult DG IPs retain embryonic DG IP characteristics, especially long-range filopodia dynamics and cellular interactions that convey Dll1+ signals throughout the SGZ niche.
source: Adult DG IPs retain embryonic DG IP characteristics, especially long-range filopodia dynamics and cellular interactions that convey Dll1+ signals throughout the SGZ niche, among other cell-contact dependent signals.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging findings from adult mice.

claim: The loss of IPs in Tbr2 cKO mutant mice, the major Dll1 source during migrations, largely accounts for premature NSC depletion, DG hypoplasia and adult neurogenesis termination phenotypes.
source: Indeed, the loss of IPs in Tbr2 cKO mutant mice, the major Dll1 source during migrations, largely accounts for premature NSC depletion, DG hypoplasia and adult neurogenesis termination phenotypes (Figures 6 and 8C; Hodge et al., 2013; Hodge et al., 2012), similar to conditional Notch inactivation phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Tbr2 cKO phenotype and comparison to Notch knockout phenotypes.

claim: DG formation has previously been shown to require the establishment of a glial scaffolding in conjunction with Notch and Reelin signaling.
source: Moreover, DG formation has previously been shown to require the establishment of a glial scaffolding in conjunction with Notch and Reelin signaling (Brunne et al., 2010; Rickmann et al., 1987; Sibbe et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The glial scaffolding was disrupted in conditional Nes-Cre/Eomes based Tbr2 cKO mutants (active at ~E11).
source: We previously found that the glial scaffolding was disrupted in conditional Nes-Cre/Eomes based Tbr2 cKO mutants (active at ~E11), whereas delaying deletion several days by using inducible-cKO Nes-CreERT2/Eomes mice and tamoxifen injection at E13.5/14.5 largely rescued the glial scaffold, although the DG anlage was still much smaller and premature NSC differentiation and depletion was still observed (Hodge et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Delaying Tbr2 deletion by using inducible-cKO Nes-CreERT2/Eomes mice and tamoxifen injection at E13.5/14.5 largely rescued the glial scaffold, although the DG anlage was still much smaller and premature NSC differentiation and depletion was still observed.
source: We previously found that the glial scaffolding was disrupted in conditional Nes-Cre/Eomes based Tbr2 cKO mutants (active at ~E11), whereas delaying deletion several days by using inducible-cKO Nes-CreERT2/Eomes mice and tamoxifen injection at E13.5/14.5 largely rescued the glial scaffold, although the DG anlage was still much smaller and premature NSC differentiation and depletion was still observed (Hodge et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Pioneering Tbr2+ Dll1+ IPs serve as the initial NSC scaffolding, and are also required to help establish the later arising glial scaffolding, in conjunction with Reelin signals from overlying CRs for organizing and maintaining later arising Notch active NSCs.
source: Hence our new data further indicates that pioneering Tbr2+ Dll1+ IPs serve as the initial NSC scaffolding, and are also required to help establish the later arising glial scaffolding, in conjunction with Reelin signals from overlying CRs for organizing and maintaining later arising Notch active NSCs, and continue to direct scaffolding changes as the DG matures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the new data and previous findings.

claim: In vitro studies would predict IP dynamic filopodia with high protrusion forces and increased (punctate) Dll1 loading would generate a strong in vivo Notch activation signal, even with incidental contacts.
source: At the cellular level, in vitro studies (Khait et al., 2016; Shaya et al., 2017) would predict IP dynamic filopodia with high protrusion forces and increased (punctate) Dll1 loading would generate a strong in vivo Notch activation signal, even with incidental contacts (Hadjivasiliou et al., 2016; Nelson et al., 2013; Seo et al., 2016; Shaya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on in vitro studies, supported by citations.

claim: Live-cell data indicate IPs undertake more directed interactions targeting contacts to nearby mitotic cells (NSCs and IPs) delivering rapid cell-cell contacts and signals between diverse progenitors.
source: However, our live-cell data indicate IPs undertake more directed interactions targeting contacts to nearby mitotic cells (NSCs and IPs) delivering rapid cell-cell contacts and signals between diverse progenitors.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging findings.

claim: Evolutionary increases in outer neocortical progenitor subtypes, as well as increases in progenitor process number are both linked to increased proliferation and expansion into outer brain regions.
source: Evolutionary increases in outer neocortical progenitor subtypes (Betizeau et al., 2013), as well as increases in progenitor process number (Kalebic et al., 2019) are both linked to increased proliferation and expansion into outer brain regions.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The early focal Dll1+ IP accumulation and subsequent pioneering DMS cohort likely provide a rich source of dynamic, probing processes mediating contact-dependent proliferation signals to later emerging NSCs.
source: Hence, the early focal Dll1+ IP accumulation and subsequent pioneering DMS cohort likely provide a rich source of dynamic, probing processes mediating contact-dependent proliferation signals to later emerging NSCs, a continuous IP characteristic in the adult SGZ niche (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' data and evolutionary concepts.

claim: Notch receptors in receiving cells can distinguish between different ligands from sending cells (trans-activation), leading to different signaling modes and downstream targets and cell fates.
source: At the molecular level, Notch receptors in receiving cells can distinguish between different ligands from sending cells (trans-activation), leading to different signaling modes and downstream targets and cell fates (Nandagopal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge supported by citation.

claim: At least canonical Dll1 and likely Jag1 activating ligands, Notch1/2/3 receptors, and Hes1/5-Hey1/2 are expressed during various stages of DG formation, suggesting different trans-activation scenarios and multiple signaling modes could mediate DNe specification, timing of progenitor migrations, and transient versus permanent niches.
source: We found at least canonical Dll1 and likely Jag1 (Nelson et al., 2013) activating ligands, Notch1/2/3 receptors, and Hes1/5-Hey1/2 are expressed during various stages of DG formation (Figure 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting different trans-activation scenarios and multiple signaling modes could mediate DNe specification, timing of progenitor migrations, and transient versus permanent niches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression data and knowledge of Notch signaling.

claim: Although IPs are a continuous Dll1 source, Notch receptor switching could also change trans-activating signaling modes and outcomes influencing quiescence, proliferation, maintenance, and neuron-astrocyte production during aging.
source: Likewise, although our data suggest Dll1+ IPs perform a continuous NSC supportive function, and adult NSCs are derived from embryonic NSCs due to constant lineage specification (Berg et al., 2019), migrating and adult NSCs change Notch receptor composition (Notch2, this study) and become activity-dependent (Crowther and Song, 2014). These observations indicate although IPs are a continuous Dll1 source, Notch receptor switching could also change trans-activating signaling modes and outcomes influencing quiescence, proliferation, maintenance, and neuron-astrocyte production during aging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed Notch receptor changes and knowledge of Notch signaling.

claim: Recent reports that Notch2 evolutionary modifications underlie outer migrating NSC expansion and diversity in human neocortex further underscore how subtle tuning of Notch receptor trans-activation and cis-inhibition can drive activity levels and promote progenitor diversity.
source: Recent reports that Notch2 evolutionary modifications underlie outer migrating NSC expansion and diversity in human neocortex (Fiddes et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2018) further underscore how subtle tuning of Notch receptor trans-activation and cis-inhibition (cell autonomous ligand-receptor interaction) can drive activity levels and promote progenitor diversity.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work on human neocortical development.

claim: Mouse DNe NSCs co-express high levels of Notch receptors and ligands (such as Dll1), predicting potentially strong cis-inhibition, yet high Notch activity was found in DG NSCs.
source: Our data show mouse DNe NSCs co-express high levels of Notch receptors and ligands (such as Dll1), predicting potentially strong cis-inhibition, yet we found high Notch activity in DG NSCs.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' data that raises a question about cis-inhibition.

claim: Oscillatory expression of Notch receptors may itself promote trans-activation between NSCs.
source: One possible explanation is that oscillatory expression of Notch receptors may itself promote trans-activation between NSCs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed high Notch activity despite co-expression of ligands and receptors.

claim: While Mib1 (a key Dll1 co-factor) promotes Dll1 trans-activating Notch signals, Mib1 abrogates Dll1 cis-inhibition to maintain Notch activity in sending cells, suggesting Mib1 could mitigate cis-inhibition in DNe NSCs while generating new IP cell fates.
source: In addition, while Mib1 (a key Dll1 co-factor) promotes Dll1 trans-activating Notch signals, Mib1 abrogates Dll1 cis-inhibition to maintain Notch activity in sending cells (Baek et al., 2018), suggesting Mib1 could mitigate cis-inhibition in DNe NSCs while generating new IP cell fates.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of Mib1 function, supported by citation.

claim: As Mib1 expression appears enriched in IPs, at least in developing neocortex, Mib1-independent Dll3 expression in late IPs could bias towards cis-inhibition and subsequent neuronal differentiation.
source: As Mib1 expression appears enriched in IPs, at least in developing neocortex (Yoon et al., 2008), Mib1-independent Dll3 expression in late IPs (Nelson et al., 2013) could bias towards cis-inhibition and subsequent neuronal differentiation (Ladi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of Mib1 and Dll3 function, supported by citations.

claim: Multiphoton live-cell data show IP dynamic processes also target contacts to neighboring mitotic IPs, even in the mature SGZ niche.
source: Interestingly, our multiphoton live-cell data show IP dynamic processes also target contacts to neighboring mitotic IPs, even in the mature SGZ niche (Figures 3–5, Videos 1–7).
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging findings.

claim: While adult DG IPs undergo limited amplification rounds at homeostasis, it is not clear whether developmental IPs are similarly limited.
source: Hence, while adult DG IPs undergo limited amplification rounds at homeostasis (Berg et al., 2015), it is not clear whether developmental IPs are similarly limited.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap, supported by citation.

claim: It may be possible to increase IP proliferative potential through targeting increased Mib1/Dll1 IP→IP cell-cell interactions to overcome Dll3 IP cis-inhibition, extending Notch activity and proliferation.
source: It may be possible to increase IP proliferative potential through targeting increased Mib1/Dll1 IP→IP cell-cell interactions to overcome Dll3 IP cis-inhibition, extending Notch activity and proliferation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the authors' findings and knowledge of Notch signaling.

claim: Stimulating one extra IP division would presumably generate a two-fold increase in neurogenic output, and potentially more due to extra Dll1+ IP processes and NSC interactions.
source: Importantly, stimulating one extra IP division would presumably generate a two-fold increase in neurogenic output, and potentially more due to extra Dll1+ IP processes and NSC interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential impact of increasing IP divisions.

claim: IP daughter cells appear to undergo significant asymmetric apoptosis during neocortical development and adult neurogenesis, which selectively limit neurogenic amplification.
source: On the other hand, IP daughter cells appear to undergo significant asymmetric apoptosis during neocortical development (Mihalas and Hevner, 2018) and adult neurogenesis (Sierra et al., 2010), which selectively limit neurogenic amplification.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Classic birth dating and chimeric studies indicated GNs in the outer GCL layers were born first, followed by GNs in the inner GCL core.
source: Classic birth dating and chimeric studies indicated GNs in the outer GCL layers were born first, followed by GNs in the inner GCL core (Angevine, 1965; Martin et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to classic studies.

claim: Pioneering IPs migrating through the FDJ-SPNZ give rise to the first set of GNs in the SPB.
source: Our multiphoton live-cell imaging and clonal lineage fate mapping results extend this early work by showing pioneering IPs migrating through the FDJ-SPNZ give rise to the first set of GNs in the SPB (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of the lineage tracing and live-cell imaging findings.

claim: As the SPB forms, additional later migrating IPs transit from the overlying SPNZ through the initial GN layer to the nascent SGZ, where their GN progeny contribute to new internal layers.
source: As the SPB forms, additional later migrating IPs transit from the overlying SPNZ through the initial GN layer to the nascent SGZ, where their GN progeny contribute to new internal layers.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging and lineage tracing findings.

claim: Subsequent IP streams continue to add GN layers, and as NSCs arrive in the nascent SGZ, locally generated IPs also begin contributing GN to internal layers of the SPB.
source: Subsequent IP streams continue to add GN layers, and as NSCs arrive in the nascent SGZ, locally generated IPs also begin contributing GN to internal layers if the SPN.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging and lineage tracing findings.

claim: After a temporal delay, the IPB forms similarly with FDJ-SPNZ IPs generating GNs in outer layers first.
source: After a temporal delay, the IPB forms similarly with FDJ-SPNZ IPs generating GNs in outer layers first.
evidence: This is a summary of the lineage tracing findings.

claim: During later embryonic and postnatal development, IP migrations begin taking a more direct route through the FDJ-Hilus to reach the SGZ.
source: During later embryonic and postnatal development, IP migrations begin taking a more direct route through the FDJ-Hilus to reach the SGZ, and multiple overlapping developmentally distinct IP cohorts converge at the SGZ to continue layering GNs internally, ultimately leaving the SGZ as the final remaining outer niche.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging findings.

claim: Multiple overlapping developmentally distinct IP cohorts converge at the SGZ to continue layering GNs internally, ultimately leaving the SGZ as the final remaining outer niche.
source: During later embryonic and postnatal development, IP migrations begin taking a more direct route through the FDJ-Hilus to reach the SGZ, and multiple overlapping developmentally distinct IP cohorts converge at the SGZ to continue layering GNs internally, ultimately leaving the SGZ as the final remaining outer niche.
evidence: This is a summary of the live-cell imaging findings.

claim: Embryonic, postnatal and adult IPs are all committed to a GN fate.
source: Importantly, our fate-mapping studies revealed embryonic, postnatal and adult IPs are all committed to a GN fate (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a summary of the lineage tracing findings.

claim: Ultimate positioning of IP-derived GNs likely depends on local influences and stochastic interactions.
source: However, multiphoton live imaging indicates ultimate positioning likely depends on local influences and stochastic interactions, since individual IPs were often observed migrating in reverse directions and adjusting routes, sometimes even migrating in circles within the nascent SGZ in a dynamic settling process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the live-cell imaging observations.

claim: Local IP positional plasticity during development may serve as a systems-level homeostatic cellular substrate contributing to GCL morphogenic robustness.
source: Hence, local IP positional plasticity during development may serve as a systems-level homeostatic cellular substrate contributing to GCL morphogenic robustness (Nijhout et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed IP behaviors, supported by citation.

claim: Longitudinal migrations (posterior/ventral to anterior/dorsal) are a potential cellular basis for ventrally derived embryonic progenitors to reach dorsal DG in the postnatal period.
source: Moreover, we also documented longitudinal migrations (posterior/ventral to anterior/dorsal), a potential cellular basis for ventrally derived embryonic progenitors to reach dorsal DG in the postnatal period (Li et al., 2013), and for NSC clonal dispersions (Berg et al., 2019; Li et al., 2013; Bonaguidi et al., 2011; Pilz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed longitudinal migrations, supported by citations.

claim: Longitudinal migrations are a potential cellular basis for NSC clonal dispersions.
source: Moreover, we also documented longitudinal migrations (posterior/ventral to anterior/dorsal), a potential cellular basis for ventrally derived embryonic progenitors to reach dorsal DG in the postnatal period (Li et al., 2013), and for NSC clonal dispersions (Berg et al., 2019; Li et al., 2013; Bonaguidi et al., 2011; Pilz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed longitudinal migrations, supported by citations.

claim: Multiple IP and NSC sources may mosaically contribute to DG formation.
source: Thus, multiple IP and NSC sources may mosaically contribute to DG formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed multiple migration routes.

claim: Tbr2+ IPs are increasingly recognized as important regulators of human brain development, as congenital EOMES enhancer mutations cause microcephaly.
source: Indeed, Tbr2+ IPs are increasingly recognized as important regulators of human brain development, as congenital EOMES enhancer mutations cause microcephaly (Baala et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study on human EOMES mutations.

claim: In addition to NSCs, IPs appear to be highly susceptible to environmental teratogen exposure in utero, such as Zika virus, which target IPs in the developing brain and cause life-long consequences for surviving infants including DG abnormalities.
source: Moreover, in addition to NSCs, IPs appear to be highly susceptible to environmental teratogen exposure in utero, such as Zika virus, which target IPs in the developing brain and cause life-long consequences for surviving infants including DG abnormalities (Ho et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2017; Nelson et al., 2020; Adams Waldorf et al., 2018a; Adams Waldorf et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on Zika virus effects on brain development.
